source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Assuming placement is correct if the client reports no discomfort, which is not a reliable method for this kind of ongoing verification","B":"Measuring external tube length at each use and assessing aspirate, rather than relying solely on the initial X-ray as the colleague is currently assuming is sufficient","C":"No further verification being needed after the initial X-ray, ever, similar to what the colleague is currently assuming about ongoing checks","D":"Listening for bowel sounds in the lower abdomen only, which is not a reliable method for confirming this particular tube's placement"}}
source_row.rationale: While X-ray remains the gold standard for confirming initial NG tube placement, ongoing verification for subsequent uses (per many facility protocols) can include measuring and documenting the external tube length at each use (comparing to the length recorded at initial confirmed placement, to help detect migration), along with assessing aspirate characteristics and/or pH when appropriate — auscultation alone (the "whoosh test") is not considered a reliable standalone verification method.
source_row.source_detail: Supportive Methods for Ongoing NG Tube Placement Verification
source_row.source_name: AACN — Practice Alert, Verification of Feeding Tube Placement
source_row.stem: A nurse needs to verify correct nasogastric (NG) tube placement before administering a feeding, and a colleague assumes that once the initial X-ray confirmed placement, nothing further ever needs to be checked again. Along with radiographic confirmation as the gold standard for initial placement, the nurse may also use which supportive method for ongoing verification?
